rows: Sediment carried (kg per hectare per year)
Trout counted per 100 m of stream

clearcutting-s2.title: A hillside before and after clearcutting

options: Cutting all or nearly all the trees in an area at one time
Cutting just the largest trees and leaving the rest standing
Burning the brush on the forest floor while keeping the large trees
Removing the tree branches that hang over roads and power lines

why.correct: Clearcutting removes every tree, or nearly every tree, from an area in one harvest.
options: Right: all the trees come down at once.
Taking only some trees is a different method, covered later in this unit.
Burning brush under standing trees is not a harvest of timber at all.
Trimming branches is not logging; the trees stay alive and standing.

items.q: Which is an economic advantage of clearcutting compared with harvesting a few trees at a time?
options: It harvests the most timber per hour of work and per trip of the machines
It keeps the stream shaded and cool for the fish that live downstream
It keeps more roots in the soil, so less soil washes off the slope
It stores more carbon in the forest each year than before the harvest

why.correct: Cutting everything at once is the fastest and cheapest way to log, which is why it is common.
options: Right: clearcutting is efficient and cheap for the logging company.
Clearcutting removes the shade, so streams warm.
Clearcutting kills the roots that hold soil, so erosion increases.
Removing the trees removes carbon storage until the forest regrows.

items.q: After a hillside is clearcut, the stream below it becomes muddy after storms. What causes this?
options: Rain falls on bare soil, runs off, and carries soil into the stream
Fallen leaves from the cut trees dissolve in the water and turn it brown
The stumps release mud into the stream as they decay over the years
Logging machines pump water from the stream and stir up its bottom

why.correct: Without roots and leaf litter, rain runs off bare soil and carries sediment with it.
options: Right: runoff from bare soil carries sediment.
Clearcutting removes most leaf litter; brown muddy water is soil, not dissolved leaves.
Slowly decaying stumps add little; the mud comes from eroded soil.
Loggers do not pump streams; the sediment is washed in by rain.

items.q: Why do cold-water fish such as trout often decline in streams below a clearcut?
options: Without shade the water warms, so it holds less dissolved oxygen
Without trees the stream gets more insects for the trout to eat
Without trees the stream water becomes salty and too dense
Without shade the trout are unable to see predators in the bright water

why.correct: Sunlight on an unshaded stream warms it, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, which trout need in large amounts.
options: Right: warmer water, less oxygen, fewer trout.
More food would help trout, not harm them; the problem is heat and oxygen.
Clearcutting does not make fresh water salty.
Light and visibility are not why trout disappear; temperature and oxygen are.

items.q: A forest is clearcut and the logs are burned at the site. What happens to the carbon that was stored in the wood?
options: It combines with oxygen and enters the atmosphere as carbon dioxide
It stays in the ashes and returns to the soil as carbon dioxide gas
It is changed into oxygen that the next forest will use for photosynthesis
It is taken up by the stumps and stored there until new trees grow

why.correct: Burning (combustion) joins carbon with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide into the air.
options: Right: combustion releases the stored carbon as carbon dioxide.
Most carbon leaves as gas when wood burns; only a little stays in the ash, and ash is not a gas.
Burning uses oxygen; it does not make it.
Dead stumps cannot take up carbon; they decay and release it.

items.q: Some foresters argue that clearcutting can help certain tree species regrow. Which statement best supports their argument?
options: Some trees need full sunlight to grow from seed, and a clearcut gives them that light
Clearcuts keep the soil shaded, so seedlings of shade-loving trees are protected
Each tree species regrows faster after clearcutting than after any other harvest
Clearcutting adds nutrients to the soil, so each seedling grows faster than before

why.correct: Sun-loving species (some pines, aspen, Douglas-fir) grow poorly in shade. A clearcut opens the ground to full sun, a little like a natural fire or windstorm.
options: Right: sun-loving species regrow well in the open.
A clearcut removes the shade, so it favors sun-loving species, not shade-loving ones.
Not every species does better; shade-tolerant trees often do worse.
Clearcutting usually washes nutrients out of the soil.

items.q: A 2,000-hectare forest loses 250 hectares to clearcutting. What percent of the forest was cut?

mistakes.why: 0.125 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for the percent: 12.5%.
That is 2,000 divided by 250. The part (250) goes on top: (250 / 2,000) × 100.

items.q: A forest stores about 150 metric tons of carbon per hectare. Write the setup for the carbon stored on 250 hectares that are clearcut, then give the answer with its unit.

why.correct: Multiply the area by the carbon per hectare so hectares cancel: $250\,\text{ha} \times \frac{150\,\text{metric tons}}{1\,\text{ha}} = 37{,}500$ metric tons of carbon.

mistakes.why: Carbon per hectare times hectares gives carbon. Multiply, so the hectares cancel.
Dividing gives a value per hectare of area, not a total. Multiply the area by the carbon per hectare.
A factor of 10 is missing: 250 × 150 = 37,500. Check the multiplication.
That would be in thousands of metric tons. Give the full number, 37,500 metric tons.

items.q: Which pair of measurements in the table shows the warmer stream also had less dissolved oxygen?
options: 18 °C with 9.0 mg/L, compared with 13 °C with 10.4 mg/L
13 °C with 9.0 mg/L, compared with 18 °C with 10.4 mg/L
40 kg of sediment with 1.8 mg/L of nitrate in the same stream
24 trout per 100 m with 260 kg of sediment in the same stream

why.correct: The clearcut stream was 18 °C with 9.0 mg/L of oxygen; the forested stream was 13 °C with 10.4 mg/L.
options: Right: higher temperature goes with lower dissolved oxygen.
These values are mixed up between the two streams.
40 kg is the forested stream and 1.8 mg/L is the clearcut stream; these are from different columns.
24 trout is the forested stream and 260 kg is the clearcut stream.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in sediment carried when going from the forested watershed to the clearcut one, then give the answer.

why.correct: $\frac{260 - 40}{40} \times 100 = 550\%$: the clearcut watershed lost 6.5 times as much soil.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, 40 kg in the forested watershed, not 260.
That is the clearcut value as a percent of the forested one (650%). Percent change subtracts first: (260 - 40) / 40 × 100.
5.5 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.
That is the change from 260 down to 40. Start from the forested value, 40.

items.q: Nitrate in the clearcut stream was 9 times higher. Which explanation fits best?
options: With the trees gone, no roots take up nitrate, so it leaches from the soil into the stream
The clearcut stream got more nitrate from rain, which falls mostly on cleared land
Trout in the clearcut stream make nitrate faster as their numbers fall
Warm water turns dissolved oxygen into nitrate in the clearcut stream

why.correct: Living roots take up nitrate. When they die, nitrate in the soil is not used and washes (leaches) into the stream.
options: Right: no uptake by roots, so nitrate leaches out.
Rain falls on both watersheds alike.
Fewer trout would add less waste, not more.
Oxygen does not turn into nitrate; nitrate comes from the nitrogen cycle in soil.

items.q: Using the table, explain why there were fewer trout in the clearcut stream.

why.correct: A complete chain names each link: the trees are gone, the stream is unshaded and warms (13 to 18 °C), warm water holds less oxygen (10.4 to 9.0 mg/L), and trout, which need cold water rich in oxygen, decline (24 to 6 per 100 m).

specific.frame: Because the stream lost ___, the water ___, so it ___, and trout ___.

cause.label: What was lost
options: the shade of the trees
its nitrate
its sediment

why.1: Nitrate rose in the clearcut stream; it was not lost.
why.2: Sediment rose in the clearcut stream; it was not lost.

effect.label: What happened to the water
options: warmed from 13 to 18 °C
cooled from 18 to 13 °C
stayed the same temperature

why.1: The clearcut stream is the warmer one, at 18 °C.

mechanism.label: Why that matters
options: held less dissolved oxygen (9.0 instead of 10.4 mg/L)
held more dissolved oxygen (10.4 instead of 9.0 mg/L)
held more nitrate for trout to breathe

why.1: Warm water holds less oxygen; the clearcut stream had 9.0 mg/L.
why.2: Fish breathe dissolved oxygen, not nitrate.

dv.label: Trout
options: fell from 24 to 6 per 100 m
rose from 6 to 24 per 100 m
did not change

why.1: The clearcut stream had 6 trout per 100 m, the forested one 24.

specific.model: Because the stream lost the shade of the trees, the water warmed from 13 to 18 °C, so it held less dissolved oxygen (9.0 instead of 10.4 mg/L), and trout, which need cold water with a lot of oxygen, fell from 24 to 6 per 100 m.

items.q: In the diagram, what keeps the stream in the forested panel cool?
options: The canopy shades the stream from direct sun
Runoff from the slope brings cold soil into it
Leaf litter on the slope cools the water as it flows
Roots pull warm water out of the stream at night

why.correct: The forest label says the canopy shades the stream, so the water stays cool.
options: Right: shade from the canopy.
Soil carried by runoff makes water muddy, not cool.
Leaf litter slows runoff and holds soil; it does not cool the stream.
The diagram shows roots holding soil, not pulling water from the stream.

items.q: Which pair of labels in the clearcut panel are linked as cause and effect?
options: "More runoff carries soil" causes the "muddy" stream
"Full sun warms soil and stream" causes "more runoff"
"Bare soil erodes" causes the stream to be "warmer"
"Nutrients leach" causes "full sun" to reach the stream

why.correct: Runoff carrying soil is what makes the stream muddy. Sun causes the warming.
options: Right: runoff carries soil into the stream and makes it muddy.
Sunlight warms the ground; it does not cause the extra runoff (bare soil does).
Erosion makes the stream muddy; the sun makes it warmer.
Leaching does not cause sunlight; losing the canopy does.

items.q: A town takes its drinking water from a river fed by the stream in the right-hand panel. Which effect on the town is most likely?
options: More sediment in the water, so cleaning it for drinking costs more
Colder water, so less energy is needed to heat it in homes
More dissolved oxygen, so the water tastes fresher than before
Less nitrate, so the water meets drinking standards more easily

why.correct: Sediment washed from the clearcut makes water muddier, and removing it at a treatment plant costs money.
options: Right: muddy water costs more to clean.
The stream is warmer after clearcutting, not colder.
Warmer water holds less oxygen, not more.
Nitrate rises after clearcutting, as the roots no longer take it up.

items.q: Which are environmental costs of clearcutting a forested hillside? Select all that apply.
options: More soil erosion and sediment in streams
Loss of habitat for animals that live in mature forest
More carbon stored on the site in the first years
Faster runoff, so floods downstream can be larger
Cooler streams that hold more dissolved oxygen
Less nitrate washing out of the soil into streams

why.correct: Clearcutting raises erosion, removes habitat and speeds runoff. It lowers carbon storage and warms streams.
options: Right: bare soil erodes and sediment reaches streams.
Right: mature-forest animals lose their homes.
Removing the trees removes stored carbon; storage falls.
Right: without trees and litter, water runs off faster.
Streams lose shade, warm, and hold less oxygen.
Nitrate leaching rises, because no roots are left to take it up.

items.q: Which situation is deforestation rather than only a clearcut?
options: A rainforest is cleared and the land is kept as cattle pasture
A pine plantation is cut and new pines grow back on the site
A storm blows down some trees in a forest that then regrows
A forest is logged and left alone so the trees grow back in time

why.correct: Deforestation is the lasting loss of forest. Pasture that is kept as pasture will not become forest again.
options: Right: the land use changes and the forest does not return.
Trees regrow on the site, so the land stays forest.
A natural disturbance followed by regrowth leaves the forest in place.
The forest is cut but allowed to regrow, so forest cover returns.
